world.setting: Contemporary American professional life: commutes, open-plan offices, home kitchens, cafes, hospital shifts, campus libraries. Everyday people, no period props.
world.register: contemporary nonfiction, explanatory, concrete everyday scenes

narrator.name: Narrator
narrator.role: the voice that frames each idea; never staged as a person
narrator.look: Off-screen narrator voice; drawn only as a calm, neutral presence, never as a face.

cruz.name: Cruz
cruz.role: the overbooked professional whose 5:20 a.m. highway crash of focus opens the book's argument
cruz.look: Cruz, a man in his late 30s, average build, short dark hair, wrinkled navy button-down shirt with the sleeves rolled up and a loosened tie, tired eyes with dark circles, holding a phone.

everyman.name: Everyman professional
everyman.role: a stand-in for any manager, freelancer, parent or student staring at a full to-do list
everyman.look: A woman in her early 40s, average build, shoulder-length brown hair tied back, plain grey cardigan over a white blouse, a lanyard badge, holding a stack of papers.

office.look: Open-plan office with rows of desks, a glowing inbox on a monitor, a wall calendar covered in colored blocks.

kitchen.look: A home kitchen at dawn: a kettle, a notebook on the counter, a half-finished to-do list on the fridge.

highway.look: A dark multi-lane highway before sunrise, one car in the passing lane, a state police cruiser in the slow lane.

cafe.look: A busy urban cafe with a laptop on a small table and a steaming cup of coffee.

classroom.look: A high school classroom with a whiteboard listing assignments and a student with a crowded planner.

hospital.look: A hospital corridor at shift change, a worker in scrubs checking a phone between patients.

library.look: A campus library reading room at night, one student alone at a large oak table with stacked books.

workstation.look: A cluttered home workstation: two monitors, a shared calendar open, sticky notes on the bezel.

objects.why: The constant interrupt: notifications that pull attention away from the one important task.
The written to-do list and the planner the book keeps returning to.
Early-morning routines and the cost of running on too little sleep.
Strategic focus: the single most important task in the middle of noise.
Time as a currency: time spent on one thing cannot be spent on another, and cannot be earned back.
Cruz's highway crash: the fast, distracted drive that opens the book's argument.
Protecting peak cognitive hours from interruptions and other people's urgent demands.
Parents and family schedules that compete with work time.
Time as a finite resource, the one asset nobody can earn back.

spine.claim: A busy professional is so overloaded that he is driving at 80 miles an hour in the dark, and he calls the overload a sign of success.
Being crazy busy is a habit of attention, not a shortage of hours, and the phone and the inbox quietly steal the time that matters most.
The people the book studied did not find more time; they decided ruthlessly what deserves their attention.
Protecting a few priority hours each day, saying no, and building shields around them changes outcomes more than any scheduling app.
Time management is a decision problem; the real question is whether we are willing to finish our most important work.
